display: Adafruit's 4.2-inch e-paper: 400x300 pixels and an SSD1683 controller. A stock refresh takes 6 seconds. How fast can it really go?
spoken: Ada fruit's four point two inch e-paper: four hundred by three hundred pixels, and an S S D sixteen eighty-three controller. A stock refresh takes six seconds. How fast can it really go?

display: Each pixel holds charged black and white pigment. Voltage pulls one color to the surface. How far the ink moves depends on voltage and time.
spoken: Each pixel holds charged black and white pigment. Voltage pulls one color to the surface. How far the ink moves depends on voltage, and time.

display: Two numbers both get called frequency. The frame rate is how often the controller scans every row and applies a voltage: 112.5 or 125 Hz. The update rate is new pictures per second.
spoken: Two numbers both get called frequency. The frame rate is how often the controller scans every row and applies a voltage: a hundred twelve and a half, or a hundred twenty-five hertz. The update rate is new pictures per second.

display: A waveform is a list of frames. Update time is frames divided by frame rate. The stock waveform spends most of its 6 seconds flashing black and white to clean the image.
spoken: A waveform is a list of frames. Update time is frames, divided by frame rate. The stock waveform spends most of its six seconds flashing black and white, to clean the image.

display: So far: stock, 0.17 fps. A custom 20-frame LUT: 3. Six frames: 11, then 15 with row-band writes. Four frames: 20. And 22 at 125 Hz.
spoken: So far: stock, zero point one seven frames per second. A custom twenty frame lut: three. Six frames: eleven, then fifteen with row band writes. Four frames: twenty. And twenty-two, at a hundred twenty-five hertz.

display: Trick one: our own waveform. Only pixels that change get pushed: 4 frames toward black, or 4 toward white. Unchanged pixels get zero volts.
spoken: Trick one: our own waveform. Only pixels that change get pushed: four frames toward black, or four toward white. Unchanged pixels get zero volts.

display: Trick two: stop paying overhead. Power up the analog side once, then send display-only updates. Turn off RAM ping-pong, and send only the rows that changed.
spoken: Trick two: stop paying overhead. Power up the analog side once, then send display only updates. Turn off ram ping pong, and send only the rows that changed.

display: Trick three: the frame rate. Our notes said 112.5 Hz was the maximum. The datasheet table goes to 125. Same four frames: 49 ms became 45.
spoken: Trick three: the frame rate. Our notes said a hundred twelve and a half hertz was the maximum. The datasheet table goes to a hundred twenty-five. Same four frames: forty-nine milliseconds became forty-five.

display: Where the 45 ms goes: 32 waiting on the panel, about 9 on SPI, about 3 in Python.
spoken: Where the forty-five milliseconds goes: thirty-two waiting on the panel, about nine on S P I, about three in Python.

display: The cost: four frames don't move the ink all the way. Black looks gray, and a ghost trail follows the square. A full refresh wipes it.
spoken: The cost: four frames don't move the ink all the way. Black looks gray, and a ghost trail follows the square. A full refresh wipes it.

display: PaperBoy is different. The M5PaperS3 panel has no controller. The ESP32-S3 drives the row and column lines itself, choosing the voltage for every pixel, every frame. It reports up to 60 fps in a small game area.
spoken: PaperBoy is different. The M five Paper S three panel has no controller. The E S P thirty-two S three drives the row and column lines itself, choosing the voltage for every pixel, every frame. It reports up to sixty frames per second, in a small game area.

display: InkBoy reached about 30 fps on a panel with a controller: a 2-step waveform, and the host gives each pixel a budget of 6 to 8 pulses for a full black-to-white change.
spoken: InkBoy reached about thirty frames per second on a panel with a controller: a two step waveform, and the host gives each pixel a budget of six to eight pulses, for a full black to white change.

display: The route for Adafruit panels, all estimates: write the next frame while the panel is busy, about 26 fps. A 2-frame LUT with per-pixel budgets, about 35. Both, maybe 50. 60 to 70 would need one frame per update, and nobody has shown that with a controller.
spoken: The route for Ada fruit panels, all estimates: write the next frame while the panel is busy, about twenty-six. A two frame lut with per pixel budgets, about thirty-five. Both, maybe fifty. Sixty to seventy would need one frame per update, and nobody has shown that with a controller.

display: Is it safe? Not proven either way. Good Display warns that pushing the frame rate too high can damage the panel. One builder saw burn-in after about 10,000 fast cycles. InkBoy warns of permanent image retention.
spoken: Is it safe? Not proven either way. Good Display warns that pushing the frame rate too high can damage the panel. One builder saw burn in after about ten thousand fast cycles. InkBoy warns of permanent image retention.

display: Keep the risk down: equal frames toward black and white, so charge balances. Zero volts on unchanged pixels. Stock voltages, datasheet frame rates. Regular full refreshes, power down when done, and no animating for hours.
spoken: Keep the risk down: equal frames toward black and white, so charge balances. Zero volts on unchanged pixels. Stock voltages, and datasheet frame rates. Regular full refreshes, power down when done, and no animating for hours.
